Question:
Which of the following is not true for myelinated nerve fibers:

Options:
A. Impulse through myelinated fibers is slower than non-myelinated fibers
B. Membrane currents are generated at nodes of Ranvier
C. Saltatory conduction of impulses is seen
D. Local anesthesia is effective only when the nerve is not covered by myelin sheath

Select the correct answer:

text:
\boxed{A}

Myelinated nerve fibers:

They are the most common type of nerve fibers in the human body. They are found in all types of nerves (somatic, visceral, and autonomic). They are of two types: a) Myelinated nerve fibers b) Non-myelinated nerve fibers

Myelinated nerve fibers are covered with a layer of myelin, while non-myelinated nerve fibers are not covered with myelin. The myelin sheath is a lipid-rich layer that is formed by the Schwann cells. It covers the axon of the nerve fiber and is responsible for the insulation of the nerve fiber.

Conduction of impulses in myelinated nerve fibers is saltatory, i.e., it jumps from node to node, skipping the myelin sheath, and hence it is faster than in non-myelinated nerve fibers.

The myelin sheath is effective in local anesthesia, as it prevents the conduction of impulses in the nerve fiber. Local anesthetics work by blocking the conduction of impulses in the nerve fiber, and thus, they are effective only when the nerve is not covered by myelin sheath.
